summary:
The Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework. The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. The courts have also intervened directly in detention: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Targeted killings of trans people continue in ordinary urban settings. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia. The assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was", and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, and the same reporting records the stabbing death of a trans woman sleeping rough.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

The source inventory records no incident, law or enforcement finding specific to Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina. A trans visitor to the islands is therefore assessed against the national position: the recognition framework set out above, and a national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence in which no arrest was recorded even after an investigation was ordered at the highest level.
tangentialFactors:
Where armed groups operate, the risk profile sharpens considerably. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through street flyers and WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, and threatened a further wave. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman reported that a friend of hers was killed. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, and Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men. A friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

National kill figures give the scale of the pattern: eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, 13 in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders were recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025. The violence documented in Caquetá and Guajira sits in territories under armed-group control, while the killing of Sara Millerey took place in an ordinary urban setting, which means neither setting is reliably protective.

No source places Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina inside either pattern, and none marks it as materially better or worse than the national baseline.
